newsitem.title: JAPAN: Ex-Soviet republics struggle to raise yen funds.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Soviet republics struggle to raise yen funds.

text.p: Failed talks between Kazakhstan and Japanese underwriters on a samurai bond issue show the difficulties that former Soviet republics face when trying to raise funds in yen, sources said on Tuesday.

The underwriters are not only worried about the new republics' low credit ratings and high political risks, but are also concerned about the negative images they have in the minds of Japanese investors, they said.
"It's not only the matter of low credit rating... Many things are involved, including unresolved territorial disputes and Russia's nuclear waste problem," one senior underwriting source said.
"The question is, can you invest in the former republics which still have many problems with Japan?" he said.
The underwriter said a long-lasting dispute over four islands seized by the former Soviet Union in the closing days of World War Two and still claimed by Japan is one of the major obstacles.

Last week, the head of Kazakhstan's central bank, Uraz Jandosov, said the bank may shelve plans to issue a yen-denominated samurai bond this summer and opt instead for another dollar Eurobond issue in the second half of the year.

Jandosov said after a presentation at the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) on April 14 that a samurai bond had been considered for Kazakhstan's second foray into the sovereign debt market, but talks with Japanese financiers had been unproductive.
"We talked with various companies, including Japanese investment banks which handle placements of samurai bonds, but these were not warm discussions," Jandosov said.

Many foreign firms and countries have floated samurai bonds and yen-based foreign bonds with their lower funding costs, and Japanese investors have bought them due to record low interest rates at home.
A record 3.92 trillion yen ($31.1 billion) worth of samurai bonds were issued in 1996, more than double the previous high of about 1.62 trillion yen ($12.8 billion) recorded in 1995.
But the situation with the republics is different, as underwriters believe there are more risks than merits.
Besides Kazakhstan, such nations as Russia, Uzbekistan and Ukraine are also considering issuing yen bonds, they said.

"Many banks and major brokerage firms have been asked to underwrite for the republics, but I think it will be very difficult to publicly place yen bonds," a senior analyst at a major Japanese brokerage said.
"Unless there is a guarantee by Japanese banks, investors are expected to turn away. A guarantee by the government of one of the republics is not good enough," the analyst said.
"If the bonds are to be launched in the Japanese market, they would have to be placed privately, targeted at investors who understand the situation in the republics very well," he added.
"We have to take a closer look at the country's fundamentals, more than the face value of the credit ratings of the ex-Soviet republics," a second underwriter said.
Rating agencies Moody's Investors Service and Standard & Poor's have given Kazakhstan Ba3 and BB- ratings, respectively, for its long-term foreign currency debt.

Japan's Finance Ministry abolished eligibility standards for issuing samurais in January 1996, opening the door for foreign issuers with sub-investment grades, which means a credit rating of below double B plus (BB+).
Since then such countries as Brazil, Mexico and Turkey have launched samurais. Romania and Argentina, which has the same rating as Kazakhstan, have also launched such bonds recently.
